# OpenMind v6 Privacy-first, user-controlled memory tools for **OpenCode V2** on Windows, Linux, and macOS — project-scoped BM25 recall, an SSRF-guarded web listener/analyzer, image and PDF reading with OCR, and optional AES-256-GCM encryption. > The npm package name is still `openmind-v5` until the registry rename lands (see [V6-ROADMAP.md](./V6-ROADMAP.md)). Local-folder installs are unaffected. OpenMind installs as a single OpenCode plugin that registers 16 tools and a bounded memory-injection hook. It never saves sessions. Durable memory is opt-in and is limited to explicit project preferences. Users can permanently delete one item, matching unwanted items, the entire backing store, or restore a previous export. The store can be encrypted with AES-256-GCM. A password is verified like `sudo`, with a 5-attempt rate limit that locks access for 5 minutes after repeated failures. For how the plugin is wired into OpenCode and where each security boundary lives, see [ARCHITECTURE.md](./ARCHITECTURE.md). ## The /listen Command OpenMind v6 ships a `/listen` slash command for web listening, learning, and analysis. The setup script copies it into your OpenCode config directory (`commands/`), so it is available after install. 1. Type `/listen https://example.com` (or just `/listen` and let the model ask for the URL). 2. OpenMind fetches that single page over HTTPS/HTTP and analyzes it: title, meta tags, Open Graph data, heading outline, links, images, code snippets, tables, lists, visible text, and a detected technology stack (React, Vue, Next.js, Tailwind, and more). 3. Add `permanent: true` (or say "remember this") to also save a summary of the findings to OpenMind memory for this project. `/listen` is SSRF-guarded — private IPs, loopback addresses, cloud metadata endpoints, `.local`/`.internal` domains, and link-local IPv6 are all blocked before any request is made — and it honors `robots.txt` (set `OPENCODE_MEMORY_IGNORE_ROBOTS=1` to opt out on a host you own). Only the URL you give is fetched: links are listed, never followed, and JavaScript is never executed, so a client-rendered page will legitimately come back with little text. The model is told to report that rather than filling the gap. ### What `/listen` Extracts - **Metadata**: title, description, author, keywords, canonical, robots - **Open Graph**: og:title, og:description, og:image, og:type, etc. - **Structure**: full heading hierarchy (H1–H6) - **Content**: paragraphs and body text, trimmed to the first 10,000 characters (2,000 with `depth: "quick"`) - **Navigation**: all external links with anchor text - **Media**: image sources and alt text - **Code**: `
` blocks
- **Data**: tables and lists
- **Tech stack**: automatic detection of React, Vue, Angular, Next.js, Nuxt, Svelte, Tailwind, Bootstrap, jQuery, WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Shopify, Gatsby, Astro, Cloudflare, Nginx, Apache, Vercel

`depth: "quick"` returns metadata, tech stack, and text only. The whole report is capped (24,000 characters, 512 KB response in quick mode, 5 MB in full mode) under one shared 30-second deadline that covers `robots.txt`, redirects, and the page.

## Easiest Install

For non-technical users, use [SETUP.md](./SETUP.md).

Windows: double-click `install.cmd`.

Linux/macOS: run:

```bash
sh ./install.sh
```

This installs the plugin dependency, registers the plugin with OpenCode, **and copies the `/listen`, `/imgread`, `/upload`, `/remember`, `/recall`, `/forget`, and `/stats` slash commands** into your OpenCode config directory. Then restart OpenCode.

To install only the slash commands into the current project instead of your global config:

```bash
node install.mjs --commands project
```

## Install From npm

After publishing this package to npm:

```bash
opencode plugin openmind-v5 --global
```

Restart OpenCode after installation. This registers the plugin only. To get the `/listen` and `/imgread` slash commands as well, run `node install.mjs` once, or copy the files in the package's `commands/` directory into `.opencode/commands/` (OpenCode reads both `command/` and `commands/`).

## Install From a Local Folder

Linux/macOS:

```bash
git clone  opencode-memory-extension
cd opencode-memory-extension
npm install
node install.mjs
```

Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
git clone  opencode-memory-extension
cd opencode-memory-extension
npm install
node install.mjs
```

Or register the plugin by hand without the setup script:

```bash
opencode plugin "$(pwd)" --global --force
```

## Manual Config

OpenCode stores global config under its config directory. You can also add the plugin manually.

Linux/macOS example:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["./path/to/opencode-memory-extension", {
      "autoInject": true,
      "injectLimit": 8
    }]
  ]
}
```

Windows example:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["C:\\Users\\you\\code\\opencode-memory-extension", {
      "autoInject": true,
      "injectLimit": 8
    }]
  ]
}
```

## Tools

- `memory_remember`: explicitly save a project memory (identical or near-identical text updates the existing memory instead of duplicating)
- `memory_update`: update text, tags, source, or the pinned flag of an existing memory by id
- `memory_recall`: search memories with BM25-style ranking; prefix a token with `-` to exclude memories containing it (a query made only of exclusions still returns the project's other memories, ordered by pin and recency). Narrow by time with `last` (`7d`), `after` or `before`
- `memory_list`: list recent memories; accepts the same `last` / `after` / `before` window
- `memory_tags`: list the tags in use for this project, most frequent first, with counts — the fastest way to find the vocabulary before a tagged recall
- `memory_stats`: report store health and shape: path, encryption state, size, store format and pending migrations, the active key-derivation function (Argon2id or scrypt) with any pending KDF upgrade, entry counts (total, visible here, pinned, stranded), oldest/newest visible memory, tag histogram, and whether the search index is built (document and term counts). It distinguishes an empty store from a locked one from memories stranded under another project path
- `memory_unlock`: verify the store password to enable encryption or access an encrypted store (5-attempt rate limit). Takes `passwordFile` (preferred) or `password`
- `memory_forget`: permanently delete a memory by id
- `memory_prune`: preview then permanently delete unwanted memories by id, text, or tag
- `memory_delete_store`: permanently delete all memories and remove the storage file
- `memory_reassign`: list and rebind **stranded** memories — records that no longer belong to the current worktree. Two kinds are recovered in bulk: memories whose recorded project directory no longer exists (renamed, moved, or deleted project), and legacy records that belong to no project at all. Memories owned by a *different project that still exists* are never taken over in bulk; they are only rebindable one at a time by naming their ids. Stranded memories are invisible to every other tool, so this is the recovery path.
- `memory_export`: show/export stored memories. `scope: "visible"` (default) exports the current worktree's memories; `scope: "all"` exports every record in the store, including legacy global-scope entries that no project can see (they are reported separately as `legacyGlobal`). The output is bounded (default 200 entries / 32,000 chars, overridable with `maxEntries` / `maxChars`) so a large store cannot exhaust the model's context; a truncated export reports `truncated` and `total`.
- `memory_import`: restore memories from a `memory_export` payload (`data` JSON text or `file`). Dry run by default — pass `confirm: true` to write. Every entry is re-sanitized and capped, `onConflict` chooses between `skip` (default), `overwrite` and `new-id`, and entries recorded against another project are refused unless you pass `reassignToCurrent: true`, and legacy global records are re-homed into the importing project (they belong to nobody, so leaving them global would make them invisible and bulk-adoptable by another project). Imported entries carry the `imported` tag and are framed as untrusted data at injection time.
- `image_read`: read an image or PDF so the model can actually *see* it — attaches the real image to the conversation and reports format, dimensions, and OCR'd text. Accepts a local path or an http(s) URL. Only image files are read; everything else is refused without revealing contents. URLs are SSRF-guarded (private, loopback, link-local, and cloud-metadata hosts are blocked).
- `memory_upload`: upload a file into project memory and save it as a project memory. Images and PDFs are read with OCR (like `image_read`); other files are read as text. The saved memory is framed as untrusted data at injection time.
- `listen_analyze`: fetch and comprehensively analyze one public website: metadata, Open Graph data, headings, links, images, code, tables, lists, full text, and detected tech stack. SSRF-guarded, honors `robots.txt`, and runs under size, deadline, and content-type limits. Backed by the `/listen` slash command.

### How recall ranks

Ranking is BM25 over a weighted bag: text counts more than tags, tags more than source, and the recorded project path is never indexed (it is a path, not content). Recall is deliberately forgiving:

- tokens are matched verbatim *and* stemmed, so `test` finds `tests` while identifiers like `redis` stay exact;
- a query term matches a longer indexed term by prefix (`kubern` → `kubernetes`);
- a one-character typo in words of five or more characters still matches (`webhok` → `webhook`), scored lower than an exact hit.

`memory_recall` only ever returns memories belonging to the current worktree.

Token bags and a term-to-memory index are built in memory on first need and
dropped whenever the store changes, so a query scores only the memories that
contain one of its terms. The index is an accelerator, not a second source of
truth: ranking is unchanged, the plain scanner is kept as the reference
implementation for the tests, and a store too large to index (over 20,000
entries, or over 2,000,000 indexed terms) uses the scanner instead of paying the
memory cost. `memory_stats` says which mode is in use.

## Image Reading

`image_read` removes the common LLM image limitations at the CLI:

- **Real image attachment** — the downscaled PNG is returned as an attachment, so the model sees the picture instead of a text description of it (capped at 8 MB per image; pass `attach: false` for metadata-only).
- **PDFs** — rasterized page by page with `pdftoppm`/`pdftocairo`, `mutool`, or `gs`, then attached and OCR'd. `pages` selects how many pages (1–5).
- **Web URLs** — downloads public images automatically (requires `python3`), streamed against a 25 MB cap and a 30-second deadline.
- **Large images** — downscales over the `max` cap (default 1400) so the model can ingest them.
- **Fine text / OCR** — runs `tesseract` directly (no Python needed) and returns the extracted text. `python3` + Pillow is the fallback path when tesseract itself is unavailable.
- **Vector images** — dumps SVG markup as text.
- **Format support** — PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WEBP, TIFF, SVG, PDF.

Examples the model can act on:

```text
Read the screenshot at ./assets/login.png and tell me what it shows.
What text is on this QR code image? /data/qr.png
Summarize the first two pages of the attached spec PDF.
Read the diagram at https://example.com/architecture.svg, no OCR needed.
```

`image_read` is deliberately refuse-by-default: it reads only image files and never echoes arbitrary file contents, so it cannot be misused as a file-exfiltration channel. If `python3` (with Pillow) is not installed, OpenMind falls back to JavaScript: it reads only the first 64 bytes to report type and dimensions, attempts OCR via `tesseract`, and URL reading is unavailable. Without any of `python3`+Pillow, `tesseract`, or a PDF rasterizer, a PDF cannot be shown and the tool says so instead of pretending.

## Known limitations

Stated plainly so nothing here is a surprise:

- No JavaScript rendering. A single-page app fetched over plain HTTP returns its shell, not its content; `/listen` reports that explicitly.
- No link following and no crawling. Exactly one URL is fetched per call.
- No proxy or custom-CA support in the fetcher; corporate TLS interception will fail the request.
- `robots.txt` is honored on a best-effort basis and fails open on network errors, which is the de-facto standard but not an access-control boundary.
- Extraction is regex-based HTML parsing, not a browser DOM: malformed markup and content assembled only by script will be missed.
- Injection is keyword-relevance ranked, not semantic. It cannot tell that "the deploy script" and "ship.sh" mean the same thing.
- Memories are private to the worktree they were saved in. There is no cross-project search; use `memory_export` with `scope: "all"` to move things deliberately, or set a shared `namespace`. `memory_reassign` will not hand one project's memories to another in bulk — only orphans whose project directory is gone.
- OCR quality depends entirely on `tesseract`; a scanned, skewed, or low-contrast document will extract poorly.
- A single attachment is capped at 8 MB and PDFs at 5 pages per call — call again for more.


## Security and VAPT

OpenMind is checked by ESLint and a GitHub Actions workflow on every push. The verification suites themselves are not published in this repository; `npm test` runs lint plus a syntax check. The properties below are what those checks cover, and what the code is written to guarantee:

- **Input injection / fuzzing** — newline-forged records, prototype-pollution tags, oversized text, regex metacharacters in queries.
- **Tampered and corrupt stores** — the plugin never crashes or leaks partial data.
- **Symlink attacks** — atomic writes replace the file instead of writing through a link.
- **Cross-process concurrency** — parallel writers never corrupt the JSONL format. A lockfile records the owner pid and host: it is stolen only when it is older than the grace period *and* the owner is provably gone, and a holder only ever removes a lockfile carrying its own token.
- **Store isolation** — two stores open at once share no vault state, key cache, or password, and deleting a store clears its lockout counters and leaves no lockfile behind.
- **Context budget** — injection is capped by total characters, not just a memory count, so one oversized memory cannot crowd out the rest; an entry that does not fit is skipped instead of ending the pass.
- **Ranking integrity** — the project path is never indexed as searchable content, and field weights keep tag hits below text hits.
- **Encryption** — AES-256-GCM authentication rejects tampered ciphertext; locked stores never disclose contents; 5-attempt lockout that only counts failures from the interactive `memory_unlock` path. The derived-key cache is scoped per store file and cleared when the password changes or the store is deleted.
- **Command injection** — `image_read` spawns the helper with an argument array (no shell); flag-like, control-character, and oversized targets are rejected up front.
- **SSRF for image URLs** — URL hosts are DNS-resolved once and any private/loopback/link-local answer (including `169.254.169.254`) blocks the fetch. The vetted address is then **pinned**: the connection dials that IP directly, so a short-TTL record cannot answer `127.0.0.1` on a second lookup. Host name, `Host` header, TLS SNI and certificate verification all still use the original name, redirects re-screen and re-pin per hop, ports are allowlisted, and proxies are disabled so the pin cannot be bypassed.
- **SSRF for web listening** — `listen_analyze` resolves the hostname with DNS and blocks private, loopback, link-local, reserved, `.local`, `.internal`, and cloud-metadata addresses before any request is made. Only `http`/`https` protocols are allowed.
- **Web fetch limits** — response cap (5 MB full / 512 KB quick), one shared 30-second deadline across `robots.txt`, redirects and the page, a strict HTML content-type gate, and bounded decompression of `gzip`/`deflate`/`br` bodies.
- **No catastrophic regex backtracking** — `robots.txt` patterns are matched as globs with a linear scan rather than a regex (a `*`-heavy rule is a measured ReDoS otherwise, and capping the star count does not fix it), and HTML containers are walked with `indexOf` rather than `[\s\S]*?`, which is quadratic on unclosed tags.
- **robots.txt** — a named group beats the wildcard group, patterns support `*` and trailing `$`, `Allow` wins ties, and the file is fetched under its own short deadline with a fail-open default.
- **Prompt injection** — a `/listen` page's prose is never stored. Only facts *about* the page are saved, with newlines, markup, and invisible formatting characters (including RTL overrides) stripped. Injected memories are fenced, the fence delimiter is escaped so a memory cannot close it, and web-derived entries carry an explicit UNTRUSTED warning that survives tag updates.
- **No content leak** — refused file types and corrupt images report a safe message, never the file bytes.
- **Errors are values** — a failing store returns a readable tool result instead of throwing out of the tool and breaking the turn.
- **Permissions** — store files `0600`; store directories are `0700`, tightened on every write even if they already existed more permissively. Temp files are created with `mkstemp` or exclusive `0600` creation, never from a predictable name.

## Encryption and Password

The store is plaintext by default for compatibility. Ask OpenCode to unlock the store with a password:

```text
Unlock the memory store with my password.
```

> **Passing a password as a tool argument sends it to your model provider** and it is normally kept in the session transcript and logs. Nothing that protects your memories needs to travel through an LLM, so prefer one of the two options below. `sudo`-style interactive unlocking is kept for convenience, not because it is the safe path.

The safe options:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["opencode-memory-extension", {
      "passwordFile": "~/.config/opencode/memory.pw",
      "autoInject": true
    }]
  ]
}
```

or the environment variable `OPENCODE_MEMORY_PASSWORD_FILE=~/.config/opencode/memory.pw` (also `OPENCODE_MEMORY_PASSWORD` for a raw secret). With either of these the store is unlocked at session start with no tool call at all, and the secret never enters the conversation. `passwordFile` refuses to proceed on non-Windows if the file is group- or world-readable.

`memory_unlock` also accepts `passwordFile` directly if you want the model to unlock on demand without ever seeing the secret. Two deliberate limits apply:

- A password file must be a regular file of at most 4096 bytes with mode `0600` on non-Windows systems. Every failure reports the same message, so the tool cannot be used to probe whether an arbitrary path exists or what its permissions are.
- Encrypting a store that is not encrypted yet, using a password file, requires an explicit `confirm: true`. Without it the tool only unlocks an already-encrypted store, so pointing it at a file cannot silently re-key your memories.

An unusable `passwordFile` in the plugin config never prevents the plugin from loading. The store comes up locked and the reason is reported in the session, rather than every OpenMind tool disappearing.

On a new store this sets the password and encrypts it; on an existing plaintext store it migrates the contents to the encrypted format in place.

- Encrypted files start with the `OPENMIND_ENC_V4` header, then an `argon2id,m=,t=,p=
` line recording the key-derivation parameters used for that file, then `salt:iv:authTag:ciphertext` (AES-256-GCM, keyed by Argon2id). Recording the parameters means a future KDF change never invalidates an existing store. Older `OPENMIND_ENC_V3` files (scrypt) and `OPENMIND_ENC_V2` files (weaker scrypt) are still readable and are transparently re-keyed to Argon2id on the next successful unlock.
- Wrong passwords are counted. After 5 failed attempts, access is locked for 5 minutes. `memory_unlock` reports the number of attempts remaining. Only the interactive unlock counts as an attempt: an ambient `OPENCODE_MEMORY_PASSWORD` that fails to decrypt does not burn the budget.
- While locked, read and write tools answer with instructions to run `memory_unlock` instead of exposing data.

To avoid typing the password each session, set it once in the environment or plugin config:

```bash
export OPENCODE_MEMORY_PASSWORD="your-password"
```

Or in the plugin config:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["opencode-memory-extension", {
      "password": "your-password",
      "autoInject": true,
      "injectLimit": 8
    }]
  ]
}
```

To keep the password out of the config file entirely, point at a `0600` file:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["opencode-memory-extension", {
      "passwordFile": "~/.config/opencode/memory.pw",
      "autoInject": true
    }]
  ]
}
```

`passwordFile` (or `OPENCODE_MEMORY_PASSWORD_FILE`) reads the password from disk and refuses to proceed if the file is group- or world-readable on non-Windows systems. Note: the password is kept in memory for the life of the OpenCode process, and its SHA-256 (never the password itself) is used as the derived-key cache key, which is scoped per store file and dropped when the password changes or the store is deleted. It is never written to the store.

`password` (inline, in config or passed to `memory_unlock`) is supported but see the warning above.

## Scopes

- `project`: the only scope. A memory belongs to the worktree it was saved in and is visible only in that project.

There is deliberately no `global` or `session` scope. Only project-scoped memories are stored; legacy global or session records created by earlier versions are ignored and never surfaced to a project. They are not lost, though — `memory_export` with `scope: "all"` includes them, and `memory_reassign` can adopt them into the current worktree.

### Session-scoped project identity (v6.3.3)

By default the OpenCode plugin instance pins the project it was created against, so a session that OpenCode later moves to another checkout still resolves to the original project.

Opt in with the plugin option:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    { "type": "local", "path": "/path/to/opencode-memory", "options": { "useSessionProject": true } }
  ]
}
```

With `useSessionProject: true`, the project key is resolved from the session's own project (its OpenCode id when available, else a stable path identity for the session directory) instead of the instance project. Recall, list, update, forget, prune, and injection all follow the same resolution.

### Moving or renaming a project

With **stable project identity** (v6.3), a memory no longer records a raw path that can go stale: the project key is a stable identity (`op:` when the instance knows it, else a `pid:` derived from the canonicalized path), with aliases tracked in the store so a rename or move keeps the memories.

Before v6.3 the memory recorded the absolute worktree path it was saved under, and rename/move made it **stranded** (invisible to recall/list/update/forget/prune until `memory_reassign` adopted it). `memory_reassign` remains the recovery path, and now also resolves short ids.

```text
Show me any stranded OpenMind memories.
Reassign all stranded memories to this project.
```

It lists candidates without changing anything, then rebinds them to the current worktree on confirmation. After that they behave like any other project memory.

Two rules keep this from becoming a cross-project takeover:

- **Orphans (bulk).** A memory is an orphan only when its recorded project directory *no longer exists* — that project is gone, so its memories can be recovered in bulk. Legacy records with no project at all count as orphans too, and adopting one turns it into an ordinary project-scoped memory.
- **Live projects (explicit only).** A memory whose project directory still exists belongs to a live project. It is never listed as an orphan and never moved by a blanket confirm. To move one deliberately, pass `includeForeign: true` to review it and then name its id: `memory_reassign({ ids: [""], confirm: true })`.

If you open the same project from several paths on purpose, set `namespace` (or `OPENCODE_MEMORY_NAMESPACE`) instead. That makes every path map to one shared project key:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["opencode-memory-extension", {
      "namespace": "my-monorepo",
      "autoInject": true
    }]
  ]
}
```

Namespace changes the stored key format to `ns:`; memories saved before the change are not migrated automatically.

## Backup and restore

`memory_export` writes JSON to the tool output, so the simplest backup is to save that output. Restore it with `memory_import`:

```text
Save this export to ~/openmind-backup.json
Import ~/openmind-backup.json into this project
```

The import is a dry run unless you pass `confirm: true`, and it reports exactly what it would write:

- **Bounded.** The payload is capped at 8 MB and 5000 entries per call; an oversized payload is refused rather than silently truncated.
- **Re-sanitized.** Every entry goes back through the same validation and caps as a fresh write (8,000-char text, 2,000-char source, 50 tags of 64 chars).
- **Project-scoped.** Entries recorded against a different project are refused by default. Pass `reassignToCurrent: true` to adopt them into the current worktree deliberately.
- **Collision policy.** `onConflict` is `skip` (default), `overwrite`, or `new-id`. `overwrite` may only replace a record this project owns; a foreign id is always given a fresh id, so an import can never delete or take over another project's memory.
- **Re-sanitized fields.** Text (8,000), source (2,000) and tags (50 × 64) are capped; control characters, bidi overrides and structural brackets are stripped from tags and timestamps, so an imported tag or date cannot forge a line that looks like another project's memory.
- **Marked untrusted.** Imported entries get the `imported` tag, which is sticky through `memory_update` and makes the injection block frame them as untrusted quoted data, exactly like `/listen` content. This is a framing aid, not a sandbox: the same text saved through `memory_remember` is treated as ordinary user data.

- **Bounded.** The export is bounded the same way the import is: `maxEntries` (default 200, cap 1000) caps how many memories are returned, and `maxChars` (default 32000, cap 2000000) caps the serialized JSON. An oversized export is truncated with `truncated: true` plus a `total` count, instead of dumping the whole store into one tool result.

`memory_stats` is the quickest way to check the result: it reports the store path, size, encryption state, and how many memories are visible here versus stranded under another path.

## Injection budget

Saved memories are injected into the system prompt on every turn. Three settings control how much:

- `injectLimit` (default 8, max 25): how many memories are injected.
- `injectMaxChars` (default 4000, max 40000): hard cap on total characters injected per turn.
- `injectItemMaxChars` (default 400): per-memory clip applied before the budget is spent.

Each memory is clipped to `injectItemMaxChars` before the budget is spent, so several short preferences always beat one long note. With the defaults an 8000-character memory contributes 400 characters instead of 8000. A memory that still does not fit is skipped, and the remaining budget is offered to the memories after it.

Selection order is pinned first, then relevance to the current user message (keyword overlap, stemmed both sides), then most recently updated. Without the relevance step the same fixed set would be injected on every turn forever.

Whenever at least one memory was considered, one line is appended *outside* the memory fence:

```
[OpenMind: injected 2 of 5 saved memories for ~/project, 3 not shown (budget).]
```

It is plain system text, not quoted memory content, so it cannot be used to smuggle anything into the fence. It exists because a silent injection failure is indistinguishable from an empty store: a full budget, a dropped set and nothing saved all used to look the same from the outside. A project with no saved memories stays silent. Turn it off with `"injectionFooter": false` or `OPENMIND_INJECTION_FOOTER=0`.

## Storage

### File format

The store is JSONL. Its first line is a version marker (`{"openmind":6}`), followed by one JSON record per line. Encrypted stores wrap the same envelope in the ciphertext instead, so a reader always knows the format before parsing entries.

Upgrades happen automatically and in place: a v5 plaintext store gains the marker on its next write, a v5 encrypted store is upgraded on the first successful unlock, and the legacy v2 key-derivation format is migrated on load. `memory_stats` reports the current format and any pending migrations.

A store written by a *newer* plugin is refused rather than parsed: every tool returns a short "newer format" message, and the file is left byte-identical. Best-effort parsing of an unknown format would drop fields and then save the truncated result, which is how memory gets silently destroyed by a downgrade.

Default memory file locations:

- Linux: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode-memory/memories.jsonl`, or `~/.local/share/opencode-memory/memories.jsonl`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\opencode-memory\memories.jsonl`
- macOS: `~/.local/share/opencode-memory/memories.jsonl`

You can override the directory with `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR`:

Linux/macOS:

```bash
export OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR="$HOME/.opencode-memory"
```

Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\.opencode-memory"
```

Or set it in plugin config:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    ["opencode-memory-extension", {
      "directory": "~/.opencode-memory",
      "autoInject": true,
      "injectLimit": 8
    }]
  ]
}
```

## Architecture

OpenMind is a single-file plugin (`index.js`) that default-exports an OpenCode V2 definition (`{ id, setup }`) and registers its tools through `ctx.tool.transform`, injects memories through `ctx.session.hook("context")`, and exports `OPENCODE_MEMORY_FILE`/`OPENCODE_MEMORY_PROJECT` through `ctx.shell.hook("create.before")`. The historical V1 factory (`MemoryPlugin`) is kept as the internal core so the test suite can drive the same logic directly. A `lib/imgread.py` helper does the image/PDF/OCR work and is spawned with an argument array (no shell). [ARCHITECTURE.md](./ARCHITECTURE.md) covers the full design: storage and encryption format, cross-process locking, BM25 ranking and the injection budget, and the network-I/O guards shared by `listen_analyze` and `image_read`.

# OpenMind architecture

How OpenMind is put together, how it plugs into OpenCode, and where each
security boundary lives. Read this alongside the `Security and VAPT` section of
[README.md](./README.md).

## 1. What OpenMind is

OpenMind is a single-file OpenCode plugin (`index.js`) plus one Python helper
(`lib/imgread.py`). It provides:

- **Durable, project-scoped memory** — an opt-in JSONL store with BM25 recall and
  a bounded auto-injection budget.
- **`listen_analyze`** — an SSRF-hardened fetcher and extractor for one public
  web page, exposed as the `/listen` slash command.
- **`image_read`** — attaches real images and rasterized PDFs to the model, with
  OCR and SSRF-guarded URL reads, exposed as `/imgread`.

OpenMind never records sessions. A memory exists only because a tool call
explicitly created it, and it belongs to the worktree it was created in.

## 2. Repository layout

```
index.js              the whole plugin: tools, store, crypto, listen, image
lib/imgread.py        image/PDF/OCR helper (invoked with an argv array, no shell)
commands/             /listen, /imgread, /upload slash commands (copied by install.mjs)
install.mjs           cross-platform setup: deps, plugin registration, commands
install.sh/.cmd/.ps1  thin launchers around install.mjs
test/                 verification suites (kept out of the published repo)
.github/workflows/    CI: lint + syntax check + load check on Node 22 and 24
```

There is no build step and no runtime dependency: `@opencode-ai/plugin` is a
development-only type source and is never imported by `index.js`. The plugin is
the source you read, and `npm install --omit=dev` installs nothing.

## 3. OpenCode integration

`index.js` has two surfaces:

| Surface | Shape | Who uses it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `export default { id: "openmind", async setup(ctx) }` | OpenCode **V2** plugin definition | OpenCode at runtime |
| `export const MemoryPlugin = async (input, options) => ({ tool, ...hooks })` | V1-style factory returning the core | the test suite, and `setup()` internally |

`setup(ctx)` is the adapter:

- **Tools** — `ctx.tool.transform((editor) => …)` re-registers every entry of
  `core.tool`, converting the historical fluent `args` builders into a plain
  JSON Schema (`makeSchema`/`tool` shim) and wrapping `execute` so its
  `{ title, output, metadata, attachments }` result becomes the V2
  `{ content, metadata }` shape (`toToolResult`).
- **Project resolution** — V2 tool context carries only a `sessionID`, so
  `projectDirectoryFor(sessionID)` resolves the session's own directory via
  `ctx.session.get(...)`, falling back to the plugin instance's location. The
  session's location is only trusted while the session still belongs to this
  instance's project (`ctx.location.project.id`): a session that was moved
  into another project keeps this instance's project, so it can neither read
  nor write that project's memories. The lookup is not cached - it is an
  in-process read, and a cached entry would keep serving the previous
  project after a move.
- **Memory injection** — `ctx.session.hook("context", …)` calls the shared
  `experimental.chat.system.transform` handler and pushes the rendered memory
  block (and any startup warning) onto `event.system`.
- **Shell environment** — `ctx.shell.hook("create.before", …)` calls the shared
  `shell.env` handler, exporting `OPENCODE_MEMORY_FILE` and
  `OPENCODE_MEMORY_PROJECT` for subprocesses.

The V1 hook names are kept as the internal interface because the tests drive
them directly; `setup()` is a thin translation layer over the same logic.

Local (non-npm) installs are registered by `install.mjs` as
`opencode plugin <root> --global --force`, which is why the README's manual
config shows a **path** entry rather than a package name.

## 4. Tool surface

16 tools, all defined once inside `MemoryPlugin`:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `memory_remember` | save/update one project memory (near-duplicates dedupe) |
| `memory_update` | edit text/tags/source/pinned by id |
| `memory_recall` | BM25 search, `-token` negation, tag filter, time window |
| `memory_list` | recent memories for this project, time window |
| `memory_tags` | tag inventory with counts, most frequent first |
| `memory_stats` | store health: path, size, encryption, counts, tags |
| `memory_unlock` | verify password / enable encryption (5-attempt lockout) |
| `memory_forget` | delete one memory by id |
| `memory_prune` | preview then delete by id, text, or tag |
| `memory_delete_store` | delete all memories and the store file |
| `memory_reassign` | rebind stranded memories (orphans in bulk, a live project's only by explicit id) |
| `memory_export` | inspect/export visible (or all) memories |
| `memory_import` | restore an export: dry-run, re-sanitized, project-scoped |
| `image_read` | attach an image/PDF plus OCR text |
| `listen_analyze` | fetch and analyze one public page |
| `memory_upload` | upload a file into memory: image/PDF via OCR, or text via read |

Every tool body runs through `guarded()`, which converts an escaping exception
into a readable tool result instead of breaking the turn.

## 5. Store, scoping, and encryption

- **Location** — `$OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR`, else the XDG/APPDATA data dir, ending
  in `memories.jsonl`. Directories are `0700`, files `0600`.
- **Scope** — project-only. A memory's `project` field is a hash of the
  worktree path (or `ns:<name>` when a namespace is set); every read filters on
  exact match. There is deliberately no global or session scope.
- **Format** — versioned JSONL (`STORE_VERSION = 6`). The first line is a
  marker, `{"openmind":6}`, followed by one JSON object per line. Encrypted
  stores begin with `OPENMIND_ENC_V4`, an `argon2id` parameter line, and
  `salt:iv:authTag:ciphertext` (AES-256-GCM) whose plaintext is
  `{"openmind":6,"entries":[...]}`. The version is known *before* entries are
  parsed, which is what makes refusal possible: a store declaring a version this
  build does not know is left byte-identical by every reader and writer.
  Plaintext lines that are not valid JSON are parsed as legacy records or
  skipped, never trusted.
- **Atomicity** — writes go through `writeAtomic` (temp file + `rename`), which
  also replaces a symlink rather than writing through it. Plaintext appends use
  an O(1) fast path with a defensive rewrite fallback.
- **Key handling** — the derived key is cached per store file, keyed by a
  SHA-256 of the password, and cleared when the password changes or the store is
  deleted. Password files must be `0600` regular files ≤ 4096 bytes, and every
  rejection reports the same message so the tool cannot probe a path.

- **Migrations** — `STORE_MIGRATIONS` is an ordered ladder of named steps
  (v5 plaintext → v6 on next write, v5 encrypted → v6 on first successful
  decrypt, legacy v2 KDF → v6 on load). The KDF layer moved from scrypt (v1) to
  Argon2id (v2) under format v4: an encrypted store written by the scrypt tier is
  transparently re-keyed to Argon2id on the next successful unlock. Each reader and
  writer checks `storeRefusal` first, so an unsupported store fails closed at every
  entry point instead of at the one that happened to parse it.

## 6. Concurrency

Two writers must not corrupt the JSONL. OpenMind layers:

1. an **in-process mutex** (`withLock`) so one event loop serialises mutations, and
2. a **cross-process lockfile** (`*.lock`) carrying `pid:host:token:timestamp`.

The lock is stolen only when it is older than a grace period **and** the recorded
owner is provably gone, and a holder removes the lockfile only if it still
carries its own token. This is covered by the concurrency verification suite.

## 7. Recall and injection

- **Recall** — BM25 over a weighted document (`text` > `tags` > `source`). Query
  terms match verbatim or stemmed, by prefix, or with one edit inside words of
  five or more characters. Negated `-terms` exclude. The recorded project path is
  never indexed, so a query naming the directory does not match everything.
- **Index** — an in-memory inverted index (`buildMemoryIndex`) caches per-entry
  token bags and a term → entries postings map. It is built lazily on the first
  ranking recall (or the first injection pass), reused for the life of that store
  version, and dropped by `saveVault` and by the plaintext append shortcut. It
  narrows *which* documents are scored, never *how*: `bm25Documents` remains the
  reference scorer, the indexed path is asserted byte-identical by the
  differential test, and stores above `INDEX_MAX_DOCS` entries or
  `INDEX_MAX_POSTINGS` terms use the scanner (the refusal is sticky for that
  store version, so it is not retried on every turn). There is
  no on-disk index, so it cannot leak plaintext from an encrypted store and
  cannot outlive the data it describes.
- **Injection** — pinned first, then relevance to the last user message, then
  recency, bounded by `injectLimit` (count), `injectMaxChars` (total) and
  `injectItemMaxChars` (per entry). Each memory is clipped before the budget is
  spent, and an entry that does not fit is skipped rather than ending the pass.
  Web-derived memories are fenced and tagged `listen`, and carry an UNTRUSTED
  warning that survives later tag updates. When anything was considered, a
  one-line provenance footer is appended *outside* the fence (count injected, of
  how many considered, how many the budget dropped) so a silent zero-injection
  is observable; it is enabled by default and can be disabled with
  `injectionFooter: false` / `OPENMIND_INJECTION_FOOTER=0`.

## 8. Network I/O guards

**`listen_analyze` / `/listen`** (`fetchPublicResource`):

- scheme and port allowlist; only `http`/`https`;
- hostname resolved once with DNS; private, loopback, link-local, reserved,
  `.local`, `.internal` and cloud-metadata answers abort before any request;
- the vetted address is **pinned** via a custom `lookup`, so a short-TTL record
  cannot re-answer `127.0.0.1`; SNI/Host/TLS stay on the original name;
- every redirect is re-screened and re-pinned under a redirect cap;
- a single wall-clock deadline covers `robots.txt`, redirects and the body;
- bodies are streamed against a size cap and decompressed with a bounded output;
- a strict HTML content-type gate, and regex-free extraction (globs and
  `indexOf` scans) to avoid catastrophic backtracking;
- `robots.txt` is honoured (fail-open on network error) unless
  `OPENCODE_MEMORY_IGNORE_ROBOTS=1`.

**`image_read`** reuses the same DNS-resolution + private-address rules for URL
targets, streams against a 25 MB cap, and spawns `lib/imgread.py` with an
argument array (never a shell). Local reads are refuse-by-default: only image
files are parsed and raw bytes are never echoed.

## 9. Verification and CI

The verification suites are maintained outside this repository, so a clean clone
contains only the plugin. Locally they are executed against the same
`MemoryPlugin` entry point and each creates its own temp store; the network
suites run against a loopback test server whose hostname resolves to a private
address, which the guard must block.

What they cover, in the order the code depends on it:

- store format, encryption, locking and cross-process concurrency;
- version headers and migrations, including refusing a store written by a newer
  build without touching it, and header-shaped memory text that must not forge
  store structure;
- ranking, negation, budget and injection keying;
- search-index parity (a randomized differential against the reference scanner),
  invalidation on every write path, and the oversized-store fallback;
- the write-path caps and the `memory_import` rules (size and entry caps,
  `sanitizeEntry`, project scoping, id-token rule, and that
  `onConflict: "overwrite"` cannot delete a record owned by another project);
- adversarial payloads: seeded cross-project records, forged output lines via
  tags or timestamps, prototype pollution, oversized or deeply nested payloads,
  and the file-read error path.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `npm ci`, ESLint, `node --check index.js`, a
module-load check and `npm test` on Node 22 and 24, so a lockfile/config drift or
a newer-than-supported API fails in CI rather than in someone's install.

# Easy Setup

This is the simplest way to install OpenMind v5.

## Before You Start

Install these first:

- OpenCode
- Node.js 22 or newer from https://nodejs.org/

## Windows

1. Download or unzip the `openmind-v5` folder.
2. Open the folder.
3. Double-click `install.cmd`.
4. Restart OpenCode.

If Windows blocks the file, right-click `install.cmd`, choose **Properties**, select **Unblock** if shown, then run it again.

## Linux or macOS

Open a terminal in the `openmind-v5` folder and run:

```bash
sh ./install.sh
```

Then restart OpenCode.

## What Setup Does

- installs the plugin's own dependency,
- registers the plugin with OpenCode globally,
- copies the `/listen`, `/imgread`, `/upload`, `/remember`, `/recall`, `/forget`, and `/stats` slash commands into your OpenCode config directory (`commands/`).

Setup needs OpenCode and Node.js 22 or newer. It never uploads anything.

## Check That It Works

In OpenCode, type:

```text
Remember for this project that I prefer short answers.
What do you remember about this project?
```

Then try the slash commands:

```text
/listen https://example.com
/imgread path/to/screenshot.png
/upload path/to/notes.txt
/remember I prefer short answers
/recall authentication
/stats
/forget <id>
```

## Optional Extras

Image reading and PDF support get better with these, all optional:

- `python3` with Pillow — image resizing, URL downloads, SVG/PDF handling
- `tesseract` — OCR text
- `poppler-utils`, `mupdf-tools`, or `ghostscript` — PDF rasterization

Without them `image_read` still reports format and dimensions, and says clearly what is missing.

## Privacy and Deletion

OpenMind v5 does not save session conversations. It stores only memories that are explicitly saved as project preferences.

Ask OpenCode to delete a specific memory, delete memories matching a tag or phrase, or delete all OpenMind memory and its storage file. Matching deletions are previewed before permanent removal.

## Optional Encryption

By default the store is plaintext. Ask OpenCode to "unlock the memory store with my password" to encrypt it. The password is verified like sudo with a 5-attempt rate limit, then the store is AES-256-GCM encrypted on disk.

## Where Explicitly Saved Memories Are Stored

- Windows: `%APPDATA%\opencode-memory\memories.jsonl`
- Linux: `~/.local/share/opencode-memory/memories.jsonl`
- macOS: `~/.local/share/opencode-memory/memories.jsonl`

To use a different folder, set `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR` before starting OpenCode.

Two security decisions in this release are worth recording:

- **`onConflict: "overwrite"` may only replace a record this project owns.** The
  first implementation keyed replacement off the payload's own `project` field,
  which is attacker-controlled; importing one crafted entry with another
  project's id deleted that project's memory. Found by red-team review during
  this release, reproduced, fixed, and pinned by two regression tests. Foreign
  ids are now always given a fresh id.
- **Imported text is untrusted text.** It gets an `imported` tag, and the
  injection fence now treats `imported` like `listen`: sticky through
  `memory_update`, and framed as quoted data the model must not obey.
- **Inline fields are sanitized, not just capped.** An independent red-team pass
  found that `tags` and `createdAt`/`updatedAt` were the only import fields
  rendered inline that were still stored verbatim, so a newline in either one
  forged an extra line that looked like a memory owned by another project

  only ids. Tags and timestamps now have control characters, bidi overrides and
  structural brackets/parentheses stripped, timestamps must parse and fit in 40
  characters, and ids are rendered through the same cleaner. `pinned` must be a
  real boolean.
- **Import cannot create a global record.** A global belongs to no project, is
  invisible everywhere, and is the one record kind another project's
  `memory_reassign` adopts *in bulk*. Accepting one from a payload was therefore
  a way to plant text a different worktree later picks up. Globals are re-homed
  into the importing project, which is also the only way they become reachable.
- **The file-read error is singular.** Directory, missing, unreadable and
  oversized all return the same message with no real size, so `file` cannot be
  used as a filesystem or file-size oracle. `memory_stats` no longer uses

  125k entries — i.e. exactly when the tool becomes useful.

### #12 was implemented without SQLite, deliberately

The roadmap said "SQLite/FTS5". The released design is an in-memory inverted
index, because FTS5 was the wrong tool for this store:

- **It would leak plaintext.** An index has to be readable to be useful, so an
  on-disk index next to an encrypted store would contain the memory text in the
  clear. Putting the index inside the ciphertext means re-encrypting and rewriting
  the entire index on every single save — worse than the scan it replaces.
- **It adds a corruption path to the one file that must not corrupt.** A stale or
  half-written index is a new failure mode with a new recovery story, for a store
  whose worst case is "the user's memories are gone". The in-memory index cannot
  outlive the data it describes.
- **`node:sqlite` is experimental and version-gated**, so the plugin's only real
  dependency would become the Node build the user happens to run.
- **The ranking is not plain BM25.** This code indexes each token verbatim *and*
  stemmed, weights text/tags/source differently, and scores against the
  *filtered* subset (tag/window/visibility filters first, so `n`, `avgLen` and
  `df` are subset-relative). FTS5's `bm25()` would silently change results.

The index keeps the observable contract exactly: `bm25Documents` is retained as
the reference implementation, `bm25WithIndex` narrows which documents are scored
(never how they are scored), and the differential test asserts identical entries,
order and scores across 400+ generated queries. Stores above `INDEX_MAX_DOCS`
fall back to the scanner rather than doubling their memory footprint.

## P0 — Correctness bugs (all reproduced)

### 1. Injection is keyed to the plugin directory, not the session directory — memories are saved but never injected

This is the headline defect: the product's core promise ("remember across sessions")
silently does not work in OpenCode V2.

- Tool write path: `index.js:2822` resolves the session's real directory via
  `directoryFor(toolCtx.sessionID)` → `ctx.session.get({sessionID})` (`index.js:2801-2813`),
  and keys the memory with it.
- Injection path: `index.js:2757-2761` builds the context from the *plugin's* load
  location (`_input.directory` / `_input.worktree`) — the directory the plugin was
  loaded from, not the directory the session is in.

Memory and injection therefore key on two different paths. `experimental.chat.system.transform`
only receives `{sessionID, model}` (confirmed in `@opencode-ai/plugin` `index.d.ts:265-270`),
so the session directory must be resolved through `ctx.session.get()` — exactly what the
tool path already does.

Reproduced: a memory saved with a session directory different from the plugin's
load directory produces `INJECTED SYSTEM BLOCKS: []`. Passing `directory` on the
transform input does not help — the handler never reads it.

Fix: resolve the session directory in the V2 `context` hook and thread it into the
transform handler; add a regression test that uses two different directories.

### 2. `sanitizeEntry` is bypassed on two write paths

`sanitizeEntry` (`index.js:1216-1239`) is the single place that enforces
`text ≤ 8000`, `source ≤ 2000`, `tags ≤ 50 × 64`. Two paths mutate entries directly:

- `saveMemory` dedupe branch, `index.js:2097-2104` — assigns `existing.text/tags/source`
  raw. Reproduced: `source` of 5000 chars and a 200-char tag persisted verbatim.
- `memory_update`, `index.js:2205` — `memory.source = args.source?.trim() || null`,
  no 2000-char cap. Reproduced: 5000-char source persisted.

A 64-char tag is a plausible prompt-injection carrier, and `source` is rendered at
injection time, so both are attacker-influenced surfaces.

Fix: run every mutation through `sanitizeEntry` (re-derive the entry, don't patch fields),
or apply the caps at the point of assignment.

### 3. A query made only of negated terms returns nothing

`filterMemories`, `index.js:1587-1638`: when `positive.length === 0` and
`negative.length > 0`, the query falls through to the BM25 branch with an empty token
list, every score is `0`, and the `.filter(doc => doc.score > 0)` at line 1627 discards
everything. Reproduced: `query: "-windows"` → `"No matching memories found."`

Negation is documented as a first-class feature in the tool description
(`index.js:2221`: "Prefix a token with `-` to exclude memories containing it").

Fix: when there are no positive terms, filter by exclusion alone and rank by
pinned/recency.

### 4. `memory_reassign` labels live memories of *other* projects as orphans

Orphan predicate, `index.js:2486-2488`:
`memory.scope !== "global" && memory.project && memory.project !== current`.
"Orphan" is inferred purely from *path difference*, so every memory belonging to a
different project is presented as an orphan and offered for rebinding. Reproduced: a
memory written in project B is listed as orphaned when called from project A.

With `confirm: true` this is a cross-project takeover primitive: a project can absorb
another project's memories. The tool's own description claims orphans are records
"that no longer matches the worktree you are in" — which is indistinguishable from
"belongs to a different project".

Fix: distinguish *moved* from *foreign*. Requires a stable project identity
(see P2 #4) — a path hash alone cannot answer it. Until then, the tool must not
present foreign-project memories as orphans.

### 5. `scope: "global"` is a dead scope

- `visibleToProject` (`index.js:1436-1439`) returns `false` for `scope === "global"`,
  so global records are invisible to every project.
- `memory_export` with `scope: "all"` filters `memory.scope !== "global"`
  (`index.js:2537`), so they are not exported either.
- `memory_reassign` skips them (`index.js:2487`).
- `memory_remember` accepts a `scope` argument, ignores it, and stores
  `scope: "project"` (`index.js:2115`), printing a note that it was downgraded.

Legacy `scope: "global"` records are stored, invisible, and unexportable. Reproduced:
a legacy global record does not appear in `memory_list` nor in `memory_export scope=all`.

Fix: either implement global scope (visible to every project, never deleted by a
project-scoped prune) or remove the argument and migrate legacy records to project
scope. Right now the API promises a scope that does not exist.

## P1 — API / correctness-of-design gaps

6. **No import/restore path.** `memory_export` exists (`index.js:2524`); there is no
   `memory_import`. A user who clears the store has no supported way to restore an
   export — and `memory_delete_store` is one confirmed call away. Add `memory_import`
   (file or inline JSON, dry-run by default, per-entry id collision policy, runs
   `sanitizeEntry` on everything it reads).

7. **No stable project identity.** Project scope is a raw absolute path
   (`makeProjectKey`, `index.js:1420-1426`). Renaming or moving a project orphans
   every memory; opening the same repo from a different path creates a second
   invisible memory space. This is the root cause of #4. Use a stable id (git
   common-dir hash / worktree id) with the path kept as a display hint.

8. **Unbounded store growth.** No entry-count cap, no TTL, no aging. Every
   `memory_remember` appends forever; `memory_recall` scores the entire history on
   every query. Add a soft cap with eviction of least-useful, least-recent entries,
   plus a `memory_stats` tool (entry count, bytes, project breakdown, oldest/newest).

9. **No per-agent or per-workspace scope.** `memory_remember` receives
   `context.agent` but ignores it. Global and agent-specific preferences are
   common enough to warrant first-class scopes (see #5).

10. **`memory_remember` silently ignores `scope`.** Either honour it or remove it
    from the schema — a silently-ignored argument is worse than a missing one.

11. **Query surface is lexical only.** BM25 over a hand-rolled stemmer is decent but
    cannot answer "what did I decide about auth?" when the memory says "login
    strategy". No fuzzy/near-duplicate clustering beyond `isDuplicate`, no
    date/temporal filters, no "recently changed" filter.

## P2 — v6 headline features (environment-verified)

### 12. Replace hand-rolled BM25 with a real full-text index: `node:sqlite` + FTS5

The current implementation re-tokenizes and re-scores the entire store on every
recall (`bm25Documents`, `index.js:1524-1585`), builds the vocabulary by scanning
every term in the corpus, and does fuzzy expansion with an O(|vocab|) prefix/edit-distance
scan per query term.

`node:sqlite` is available on this host and fully featured — verified on Node v24.21.0:
`DatabaseSync` present, **FTS5**, **trigram tokenizer**, and **json1** all working.
FTS5 gives: a real inverted index (no full-corpus rescan), prefix queries
(`token*`), BM25 ranking built in, `trigram` for substring/fuzzy matching,
`snippet()`/`highlight()` for previews, and `json1` for querying structured columns
(tags, scope, pinned) inside the index.

Plan: keep the JSONL store as the source of truth (portability + existing backup
story) and maintain a derived SQLite FTS index rebuilt from it, or migrate to a
SQLite primary store with a JSONL export path. Must handle: index corruption →
rebuild from JSONL; lock contention with the existing file lock; encrypted stores
(plaintext index on disk would leak memory text — index must live inside the
encrypted container or be rebuilt in a temp file and deleted).

### 13. Semantic / hybrid recall — **in progress (v6.5.0)**

Started: the recall tool now accepts a `mode` (`keyword` default, `semantic`,
`hybrid`), ranks through a local embedding seam (`embedTexts` / `setSemanticEmbedder`),
computes cosine similarity, and fuses the embedding ranking with the BM25 ranking
via reciprocal rank fusion (`reciprocalRankFusion`) for hybrid mode.

Remaining for the milestone: wire the actual local embedding model behind the seam,
then ship. Keyword behaviour is unchanged and pinned by the existing suites.

Add embedding-backed recall, combined with FTS/BM25 via reciprocal rank fusion
(RRF), which needs no score calibration between the two rankers. Storage: a small
vector column (or a sidecar file) alongside each memory, plus a `memory_recall`
mode flag (`keyword | semantic | hybrid`). Embeddings must be computed locally
(no network, no provider key) — a small ONNX/transformers model is the sane
default; an optional remote embedder behind an explicit opt-in flag if desired.
Must remain compatible with the encrypted store (vectors are derived data and leak
text; keep them inside the encrypted payload or regenerate).

### 14. KDF upgrade: scrypt → Argon2id — **shipped in 6.4.0**

Current KDF: Argon2id (`m=64 MiB, t=3, p=1`), header `OPENMIND_ENC_V4`, AES-256-GCM,
5-attempt / 5-minute lockout.

Shipped: `crypto.argon2` / `crypto.argon2Sync` are present on Node v24.21.0, so the
KDF runs in-process with no native dependency. The store format moved to
`OPENMIND_ENC_V4` with versioned Argon2id parameters; scrypt-tier stores
(`OPENMIND_ENC_V3` / `OPENMIND_ENC_V2`) are transparently re-keyed to Argon2id on
the next successful unlock (decrypt with the old KDF, re-encrypt with the new one).

### 15. Publish to npm

The package is **not published**: `npm view openmind` → 404 and
`npm view openmind-v5` → 404 (checked 2026-10-21). The remote is
`git@github.com:Mithil0605/openmind.git`. Publishing removes the
`opencode plugin <absolute-path> --global --force` install requirement from
`install.mjs` and makes version upgrades possible for other users. Decide the
package name (`openmind` is likely taken; `opencode-memory-extension` or
`openmind-v6`), ship a `bin` CLI (`openmind init|doctor|export|import|reindex`)
and a `postinstall` that does not touch global config silently.

### 16. Store format v6 + migrations

Introduce an explicit store version and a migration runner
(`V1 flat JSON → V2 legacy lines → V3 encrypted → v6 index`), so upgrades are
testable and rollback is possible. Include a `migration` test that materializes
each historical fixture and asserts the v6 result.

description: Forget a specific memory
---

Delete a specific memory using the OpenMind `memory_forget` tool.

1. Take the memory id from `$ARGUMENTS`. If empty, ask for the id (short or full) and stop until the user answers.
2. If the user wants to delete multiple, or isn't sure which id to use, call `memory_recall` or `memory_list` first to show candidates and their ids/scopes.
3. Call `memory_forget` with `ids` containing the id(s) the user confirmed.
4. Report what was deleted. If nothing matched, say so clearly.
5. For bulk deletions by tag/phrase, use `memory_prune` (it shows a preview unless confirmed) — don't guess.

---
description: Read an image or PDF into the conversation with OCR, using the OpenMind image_read tool
---

When /imgread is invoked, make an image or PDF readable by the model.

1. Take the path or URL from `$ARGUMENTS`. If it is empty, ask for it and stop
   until the user answers.
2. Call the OpenMind `image_read` tool with `target: <path-or-url>`. It returns
   the real image as an attachment plus format, dimensions and OCR text.
   - `max`: cap for the longest side before downscaling (default 1400, max 4096).
   - `ocr`: runs by default; pass `ocr: false` only for speed or when the image
     has no text.
   - `attach`: default true. Leave it on — without the attachment the model
     cannot actually see the image.
   - `pages`: for PDFs, how many pages to rasterize and OCR (default 1, max 5).
   - `attach: false` returns text and metadata only, without pixels.
3. If the tool reports that python3 is missing, or the format is unsupported,
   say so plainly and tell the user what to install (python3 with Pillow and
   tesseract, or poppler-utils/mupdf/ghostscript for PDFs). Do not claim to have
   seen an image you could not read.
4. Report what is visible: subject, embedded or OCR'd text, dimensions, and
   format. Never invent details that are not in the image.

description: Fetch and analyze a public website with listen_analyze, optionally saving findings to OpenMind memory
---

When /listen is invoked, analyze a website with the OpenMind `listen_analyze`
tool.

1. Take the URL from `$ARGUMENTS`. If it is empty, ask the user for one URL and
   stop until they answer.
2. Call `listen_analyze` with:
   - `url`: the URL the user gave.
   - `depth`: `"quick"` for metadata + tech stack + text only, `"full"`
     (default) for headings, links, images, code blocks, tables and lists.
   - `permanent`: `true` only when the user asked to remember the site, `false`
     for a one-time read. Do not save anything the user did not ask to save.
3. Present the result faithfully: title/description/Open Graph, heading outline,
   detected tech stack, the visible text and any code or tables, plus notable
   links. Quote the page; do not add facts the fetch did not return.
4. Report the tool's own warnings when present: a robots.txt refusal, a
   client-rendered page that returned almost no text, a non-HTML content type, or
   a truncated report.
5. If `permanent` was true, tell the user the memory id that was saved, and
   note that it is a project-scoped memory they can delete with `memory_forget`
   or `memory_delete_store`.

Notes: the tool honors robots.txt, refuses private/loopback/link-local and
cloud-metadata hosts, executes no JavaScript, and follows no links — only the
single URL given is fetched.

description: Recall memories for this project
---

Recall memories for the current project using the OpenMind `memory_recall` tool.

1. Take the query from `$ARGUMENTS`. If empty, show recent memories using `memory_list` instead (or ask for a query).
2. Call `memory_recall` with:
   - `query`: the text/keywords the user wants (supports `-term` to exclude)
   - `tags`: only if the user wants to filter to specific tags
   - `limit`: only if the user asked for a specific number (default 10, max 50)
   - `mode`: only if the user asked for semantic or hybrid recall (default `keyword`)
   - `last`/`after`/`before`: only if the user asked about a time window
3. Present the results as shown by the tool (ids, scope, tags, pinned, timestamp). If there are no matches, say so plainly.
4. If the user says "why was X injected" or seems confused, suggest `memory_inspect <id>` or `/stats` to debug.

Remember a durable project fact using the OpenMind `memory_remember` tool.

2. Present the full result as returned (path, encryption, size, format/migrations, counts, oldest/newest, tags, index state).
3. If it reports stranded/legacy memories, suggest `memory_reassign` (preview first).

description: Upload a file into OpenMind memory with memory_upload
---

When /upload is invoked, turn a file the user wants remembered into a durable OpenMind memory.

1. Take the target (a local path or an http(s) URL) from `$ARGUMENTS`. If it is empty, ask for the file and stop until the user answers.
2. Prefer a local path: the user attached or saved a file. Accept a URL only when the user explicitly gave a web link.
3. Call the OpenMind `memory_upload` tool with:
   - `target`: the path or URL to upload.
   - `ocr`: default true; pass `ocr: false` only for text files or for speed.
   - `max`: cap for OCR/downsampling (default 1400, max 4096).
4. Present what was saved: the memory id, plus a short faithful summary of the extracted content. Do not dump raw file content into the conversation.
5. Tell the user the memory is framed as untrusted data and how to remove it: `memory_forget`, `/forget`, or `memory_delete_store`.

Notes: images and PDFs are read with OCR (python3 + Pillow/tesseract, or a PDF rasterizer); other files are read as text. Only extracted text becomes a memory — raw bytes never do.
